caption: Marcus v. Search Warrant
justification: PAGE CANDIDATE. Missing controlling SCOTUS expressive-material warrant case. Search warrants for all obscene material, issued without judicial review of the publications and leaving selection to officers, lacked the safeguards required when a warrant/seizure burdens protected expression; directly fills the Stanford/particularity expressive-material warrant line.

caption: Lee Art Theatre, Inc. v. Virginia
justification: PAGE CANDIDATE. Missing controlling SCOTUS probable-cause-in-affidavit case for expressive-material warrants. A warrant based only on a police officer's conclusory obscenity assertion, without the magistrate probing the factual basis, was constitutionally insufficient and the seized films were inadmissible.

caption: Heller v. New York
justification: PAGE CANDIDATE. Missing controlling SCOTUS execution/remedy limit for seizure of allegedly obscene films. A single evidentiary copy may be seized under an ex parte warrant after a neutral magistrate's probable-obscenity determination if a prompt adversary hearing is available and copying/return safeguards protect continued exhibition.

caption: Roaden v. Kentucky
justification: PAGE CANDIDATE. Missing controlling SCOTUS warrant-requirement and suppression case. A sheriff's warrantless seizure of a film after viewing it was unreasonable; expressive-material seizures require prior judicial approval absent true now-or-never exigency, and the film should have been suppressed.

caption: New York v. P. J. Video, Inc.
justification: PAGE CANDIDATE. Missing controlling SCOTUS standard-of-probable-cause case for warrants targeting presumptively protected materials. The First Amendment does not impose a higher probable-cause standard; Gates fair probability governs, while the application still must give the magistrate enough factual basis to judge obscenity.

caption: Fort Wayne Books, Inc. v. Indiana
justification: PAGE CANDIDATE. Missing controlling SCOTUS expressive-material seizure boundary. Mere probable cause to believe expressive materials are obscene or tied to racketeering cannot support pretrial seizure of an entire bookstore and contents; final obscenity adjudication is required before removing expressive inventory from circulation.
